migrationNotes: Spine: an organiser's results board has to say what a tie means, so a race with a joint winner is followed from numbering every row, to sharing a place, to ranks with and without gaps, to breaking the tie with a second column.

Left out of the lesson (still in the course): sql-rank-with-ties-1 (what a window calculation preserves) and -9 (why order 103 gets rank 3). The first screen teaches the first and the second screen teaches the second.

lesson.title: Rank rows without collapsing them

lead.text: Earlier lessons collapsed rows. GROUP BY turns a table of orders into one line for each customer, and the individual orders disappear into their totals. A results board can't work like that, because every runner needs a line of their own with a position beside it. What the board needs is a calculation that adds a value to each row and leaves the rows where they are.

That is what a window function does. The window is the set of rows the calculation is allowed to look at, and the function works out its value for one row at a time. You write it as the function followed by OVER, with the order to use in brackets. The simplest is ROW_NUMBER, which hands out 1, 2, 3 down the rows in the stated order.

afterFigure.text: The figure sets the two side by side on the shop's orders. The grouped query returns three lines, one for each customer. The window query returns all six orders, each with its position. The ORDER BY inside the brackets decides which row counts as first, so the numbering is only as sensible as that order is. A different ORDER BY would number the same rows differently.

queries.label: Grouped
queries.sql: SELECT customer_id, COUNT(*) AS orders FROM orders GROUP BY customer_id ORDER BY customer_id;

queries.label: Windowed
queries.sql: SELECT id, customer_id, ROW_NUMBER() OVER (ORDER BY id) AS position FROM orders ORDER BY id;

lead.text: The ORDER BY inside OVER decides who counts as first.

ROW_NUMBER always separates the rows. When two rows are equal it still gives one of them the smaller number, and the choice between them is arbitrary. A results board wants something different for a tie: equal rows should get equal positions.

RANK does that. Rows that tie get the same rank, and the next row's rank is one more than the number of rows ahead of it. Picture a diving contest in which Eve, Fay and Gus all score 9 and Hal scores 7. The three at the top share first place. Three divers are ahead of Hal, which makes him fourth. Nobody is second or third, and the gap is deliberate, because the rank says how many divers finished ahead.

afterFigure.text: The figure gives the same contest both ways. ROW_NUMBER splits the three top scorers into 1, 2 and 3, while RANK puts all three on 1 and then jumps to 4. Counting the rows ahead is the whole rule, so you can check any rank by counting how many rows have a better value and adding one.

queries.label: Every row numbered
queries.sql: SELECT name, points, ROW_NUMBER() OVER (ORDER BY points DESC, name) AS position FROM divers ORDER BY position;

queries.label: Tied rows share a rank
queries.sql: SELECT name, points, RANK() OVER (ORDER BY points DESC) AS position FROM divers ORDER BY position, name;

lead.text: Use the rule from the diving contest. Count the runners who finished ahead.
Order the amounts largest first, then count the rows that come before the 40.

reveal.text: You counted the rows ahead and added one. Ties are part of that count, which is why RANK can leave gaps.

queries.label: Number each row
queries.sql: SELECT id, amount, ROW_NUMBER() OVER (ORDER BY amount DESC, id ASC) AS position FROM orders WHERE amount IS NOT NULL ORDER BY amount DESC, id ASC;

queries.label: Share ranks for equal amounts
queries.sql: SELECT id, amount, RANK() OVER (ORDER BY amount DESC) AS position FROM orders WHERE amount IS NOT NULL ORDER BY amount DESC, id ASC;

lead.text: RANK's jump from 1 to 4 suits a results board, because a place says how many finished ahead. A table of prizes can need the opposite. If prizes go to first and second place, a diver behind the three joint leaders should still take second, with no missing positions.

DENSE_RANK does that. Tied rows share a rank, as they do under RANK, but the next rank is just one more than the previous rank, whatever the size of the tie. It counts different values ahead and adds one, where RANK counts rows ahead and adds one. Hal is second, because only one different score, 9, is higher than his 7.

afterFigure.text: The figure puts the two side by side. The top three get 1 under both. Under RANK Hal is 4th, and under DENSE_RANK he is 2nd. Neither rule is wrong, since the right choice depends on what a position should mean in the report.

queries.label: Ranks with gaps
queries.sql: SELECT name, points, RANK() OVER (ORDER BY points DESC) AS position FROM divers ORDER BY position, name;

queries.label: Ranks without gaps
queries.sql: SELECT name, points, DENSE_RANK() OVER (ORDER BY points DESC) AS position FROM divers ORDER BY position, name;

lead.text: Count the different amounts above the 40, then add one.

reveal.text: You counted different amounts, not rows. Choose RANK or DENSE_RANK by what the report should mean.

queries.label: Ranks with gaps
queries.sql: SELECT id, amount, RANK() OVER (ORDER BY amount DESC) AS position FROM orders WHERE amount IS NOT NULL ORDER BY amount DESC, id ASC;

queries.label: Ranks without gaps
queries.sql: SELECT id, amount, DENSE_RANK() OVER (ORDER BY amount DESC) AS position FROM orders WHERE amount IS NOT NULL ORDER BY amount DESC, id ASC;

lead.text: A tie is only a tie while the window can't tell two rows apart. The window compares rows using everything inside its ORDER BY, so a second column can separate rows that the first leaves level. Eve, Fay and Gus all scored 9, but their names differ, and putting the name after the score tells the window how to put them in order.

With that second column in place the three are no longer equal. RANK now gives them 1, 2 and 3, because each has a different number of divers ahead of it, and Hal stays fourth. The result looks just like ROW_NUMBER's, which gives a useful rule of thumb. If the ORDER BY puts every row in a different place in the line, the ties are gone and ROW_NUMBER, RANK and DENSE_RANK all agree.

afterFigure.text: The figure ranks the contest twice. The first query orders by points alone, so the three scores of 9 tie. The second adds the name, and the tie breaks into three separate places. Add a tie-breaker when a report must pick exactly one winner, and leave it out when equal values really should share a place.

queries.label: Points only
queries.sql: SELECT name, points, RANK() OVER (ORDER BY points DESC) AS position FROM divers ORDER BY position, name;

queries.label: Points, then name
queries.sql: SELECT name, points, RANK() OVER (ORDER BY points DESC, name) AS position FROM divers ORDER BY position;

lead.text: The window compares rows by everything in its ORDER BY. Think about what an extra column does to two rows that are level.

queries.label: Rank the amount
queries.sql: SELECT id, amount, RANK() OVER (ORDER BY amount DESC) AS position FROM orders WHERE amount IS NOT NULL ORDER BY amount DESC, id ASC;

queries.label: Rank amount and id
queries.sql: SELECT id, amount, RANK() OVER (ORDER BY amount DESC, id ASC) AS position FROM orders WHERE amount IS NOT NULL ORDER BY amount DESC, id ASC;

lesson.orientation: Distinguish ROW_NUMBER, RANK and DENSE_RANK and choose tie behaviour deliberately.
lesson.nextAction: Apply the idea to the next query.

blocks.text: Four runners cross the finish line in 10, 10, 12 and 14 seconds. The two fastest reach it together, so the organiser's results board has to say something about the tie. The rule is that runners with equal times share a place.

That is easy to say and awkward to write down. If two runners share first place, the next runner is third by some ways of counting and second by others, and the board has to follow a single rule for everyone. The last runner's place depends on which rule it is.

Ranking the rows of a table raises the same choice. A report that lists every row with a position beside it needs a rule for equal values, and SQL offers several. This lesson numbers the rows first and then follows the race's tie through each rule.

intro.promise: By the end you'll put a position beside every row and say how each way of numbering treats ties.

recap.keyIdea: A window function ranks rows without collapsing them. ROW_NUMBER never ties. RANK leaves gaps after ties, and DENSE_RANK does not.

blocks.text: You placed the 14-second runner 4th, then ranked the amount 40 as 3 with RANK and 2 with DENSE_RANK. Adding id to the ordering split the tie at 80.

recap.nextHook: Every ranking so far treated the table as one race. Often the rows belong to separate groups that should each be ranked or totalled on their own, like the pupils of different classes on one mark sheet. The next lesson splits a window into groups.

questions.prompt: What does a window calculation preserve here?
hints: Compare the five-row window result with the grouped result.

answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: A window calculation adds a result to each retained order row. Unlike GROUP BY aggregation, it does not collapse the rows into one row per group.

questions.onCorrect: Each individual known order row. A window calculation adds a value without collapsing rows.

misconceptions.feedback: That is what GROUP BY does. A window calculation keeps the rows.
Nothing is filtered out. Every known order stays.

questions.prompt: The shop's known order amounts are 80, 20, 80, 40 and 20. Under RANK() OVER (ORDER BY amount DESC), what rank does the amount 40 receive?
hints: Count rows with greater amounts.
Ordinary rank is one plus the number of preceding higher-valued rows.
Ordinary rank equals one plus the number of rows whose amount is greater.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: Two 80 rows share rank 1, so the next row's rank is 3.

questions.onCorrect: 3. Two rows have a greater amount, so RANK is one plus that count.

misconceptions.feedback: That is the dense rank. RANK counts the rows that come before, ties included.
Count how many rows have a greater amount, then add one.

questions.prompt: The shop's known order amounts are 80, 20, 80, 40 and 20. Under DENSE_RANK() OVER (ORDER BY amount DESC), what rank does the amount 40 receive?
hints: Dense ranks count different preceding values.
There is one distinct amount greater than forty.
Dense rank equals one plus the number of distinct greater amount values.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: 80 is the first distinct amount; 40 is the second.

questions.onCorrect: 2. One different amount is greater, so DENSE_RANK is one plus that count.

misconceptions.feedback: That is the plain rank. Dense ranks count different values.

questions.prompt: On the shop's amounts, orders 101 and 103 tie at 80. What happens to that tie if id is added inside the ranking window's ORDER BY?
hints: The window compares the complete ordering tuple.

acceptedIdeas: The two rows no longer tie
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Window ties depend on every ORDER BY expression. Adding distinct ids makes the two 80 rows different ordering keys, so they no longer tie.

choices.label: The two rows no longer tie
Both rows must still have rank 1

questions.onCorrect: The two rows no longer tie. Adding id makes every order different in the window.

misconceptions.feedback: The window now compares id too, so the amounts no longer tie.

questions.prompt: Amounts sorted descending are 90, 90, 70, 50. What is RANK for 70?
hints: Ordinary rank includes gaps after ties.
There are two preceding higher-valued rows.
Count the two rows with 90, then add one for the next row's ordinary rank.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: Two higher rows precede 70, so its ordinary rank is 3.

questions.onCorrect: 3. Two rows with 90 come before it, so RANK is one more than that.

misconceptions.feedback: That counts only the different greater values. RANK counts rows ahead.
Count the rows with a greater amount, then add one.

questions.prompt: Type the function name that gives every row a separate position in the specified order.
hints: This function assigns consecutive positions even when values tie.

answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: ROW_NUMBER assigns a separate consecutive position to every row in the window's specified order. A unique tie-breaker makes that order deterministic.

questions.onCorrect: ROW_NUMBER. It gives every row its own consecutive position.

misconceptions.feedback: That gives tied rows the same position. The one wanted separates every row.

questions.prompt: Four runners finish in 10, 10, 12 and 14 seconds. Runners with equal times share a place. What place does the 14-second runner get?
hints: Two runners share first place.
How many runners finished ahead of the 14-second runner?
Add one to the number of runners ahead.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: Two runners tie for first, and one more finishes ahead of the 14-second runner. Three runners are ahead, so fourth place.

questions.onCorrect: 4. A place counts the runners ahead of you, ties included. RANK works the same way.

misconceptions.feedback: That counts the different times. A place counts the runners who finished ahead.

questions.prompt: The amounts are 30, 10 and 20. With ROW_NUMBER() OVER (ORDER BY amount DESC), which amount gets number 1?
hints: Which direction does DESC use?
The first row in the stated order gets number 1.
Which amount comes first, largest first?

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: DESC puts the largest amount first, so 30 is numbered 1.

questions.onCorrect: 30. The ORDER BY inside OVER sets the order, and the first row in that order gets number 1.

misconceptions.feedback: That is the smallest. DESC puts the largest first.

questions.prompt: Why does order 103 get rank 3 and not 2?
hints: How many rows come before order 103?

acceptedIdeas: Two rows come before it, so its rank is one more than that.
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Orders 101 and 102 come before it, so its rank is two plus one.

questions.onCorrect: RANK is one plus the number of rows that come before, ties included.

choices.label: Two rows come before it, so its rank is one more than that.
Rank counts the different customer ids only.

misconceptions.feedback: RANK counts rows ahead, not different values.
Ranks are not used up. A rank comes from how many rows are ahead.

questions.prompt: Amounts sorted descending are 90, 90, 70 and 50. What is DENSE_RANK for 70?
hints: DENSE_RANK never skips a number.
How many different amounts are greater than 70?
Add one to the number of different greater values.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: One different amount, 90, is greater than 70. Dense rank counts values, so it is one plus one.

questions.onCorrect: 2. DENSE_RANK counts different greater values, so tied rows do not push the next rank up.

misconceptions.feedback: That is the plain RANK, which counts rows ahead. DENSE_RANK counts different values.
